# Robust marginalization of baryonic effects for cosmological inference at the field level

## Abstract

We train neural networks to perform likelihood-free inference from $(25\,h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^{2}$ 2D maps containing the total mass surface density from thousands of hydrodynamic simulations of the CAMELS project. We show that the networks can extract information beyond one-point functions and power spectra from all resolved scales ( $\gtrsim 100\,h^{-1}{\rm kpc}$ ) while performing a robust marginalization over baryonic physics at the field level: the model can infer the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}(\pm 4\%)$ and $\sigma_{8}(\pm 2.5\%)$ from simulations completely different to the ones used to train it.

The wealth and quality of data from upcoming surveys such as DESI [1], eRosita [2], Euclid [3], PFS [4], SKA [5], Roman [6], and Rubin [7] is expected to bring cosmology to a different level. The data from these surveys contain the key to answering fundamental questions in physics such as what the nature of dark energy or the sum of the neutrino masses are. The main obstacle to achieving this is not the amount and quality of data, but two significant theoretical challenges: 1) the optimal summary statistic(s) needed to extract the maximum amount of information from data in the mildly and fully non-linear regimes is unknown, and 2) astrophysical processes such as feedback from supernovae and active galactic nuclei (AGN) are expected to impact the non-linear regime in a poorly understood manner.

Ideally, one would want to use an estimator that is able to extract the maximum amount of information directly from the field while marginalizing over baryonic effects at the same time. In [8] we demonstrated with toy examples that neural networks can achieve both goals. In our companion paper [9] we have shown that neural networks can extract cosmological information embedded in state-of-the-art hydrodynamic simulations from complex 2D fields such as gas temperature, electron number density, and magnetic fields, while marginalizing over baryonic effects at the same time.

In this letter we show, for the first time, that this procedure can be robust. In other words, it does not rely on training or testing the model on a particular type of simulation. We will show that neural networks trained on total matter surface density maps from one suite of simulations can infer the correct cosmology even when tested on maps from another suite, and vice versa. It is not obvious that this should work, because the two suites follow a different set of hydrodynamic equations, use distinct numerical methods to solve them, and employ different subgrid models. We also show that rather than simply extracting cosmological information only from large scales to avoid bias, our networks successfully extract cosmological information from the smallest scales resolved in the maps. These results have important consequences for weak lensing surveys, paving the way to a method that can extract all information from the field while marginalizing over baryonic effects.

We use data from the Cosmology and Astrophysics with MachinE Learning Simulations (CAMELS) project [10] at $z=0$ . CAMELS contains two simulation suites, IllustrisTNG and SIMBA, which have been run using the AREPO [11] and GIZMO [12] codes, employing the subgrid physics implemented in the IllustrisTNG [13, 14] and SIMBA [15] simulations, respectively. For each suite, we use the latin-hypercube (LH) set, which contains 1,000 simulations, each with a different value of the cosmological parameters $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ , the fractional matter density and the amplitude of fluctuations in spheres of radius 8 $h^{-1}{\rm Mpc}$ , and four astrophysical parameters controlling the efficiency of supernova and AGN feedback ( $A_{\rm SN1}$ , $A_{\rm SN2}$ , $A_{\rm AGN1}$ , $A_{\rm AGN2}$ ) as well as a different value of the random seed used to generate the initial conditions. The value of the cosmological and astrophysical parameters is varied across a very wide range; e.g. $\Omega_{\rm m}\in[0.1,0.5]$ and $\sigma_{8}\in[0.6,1.0]$ . We refer the reader to [10] for further details on the CAMELS simulations.

From these simulations we generate 2D total mass surface density maps as follows. First, we take slices of dimensions $25\times 25\times 5~(h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^{3}$ and project all particle positions in the slice into the 2D plane along the third axis. We then assign the particle positions and their masses to a 2D regular grid with $256\times 256$ pixels, considering that each particle represents a circle with uniform density within its radius. For gas and dark matter particles this radius is set to the distance from the particle to its 32nd nearest neighbor, while stars and black holes are considered to be point masses. Finally, we divide the projected mass in every pixel by its area to obtain the total mass surface density. For each simulation we produce 15 maps, giving rise to 15,000 maps for the IllustrisTNG simulations, and another 15,000 maps for the SIMBA simulations. In Fig. 1 we show a few examples of these maps. We provide further details on the method used to generate the maps in our companion paper [16].

We use these maps to train moment neural networks [17] to infer the values of the marginal posterior mean ( $\mu_{i}$ ) and standard deviation ( $\sigma_{i}$ ) for each parameter $\theta_{i}$ . The output of the network is thus twelve numbers, two per parameter. The loss function we optimize via gradient descent is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{6}\log\left(\sum_{j\in{\rm batch}}\left(\theta_{i,j}-\mu_{i,j}\right)^{2}\right) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{6}\log\left(\sum_{j\in{\rm batch}}\left(\left(\theta_{i,j}-\mu_{i,j}\right)^{2}-\sigma_{i,j}^{2}\right)^{2}\right)~, $$

where the interior sum runs over all maps in the batch while the external sum runs over all six parameters.

Our architecture consists in a set of 6 blocks, where each block follows the structure CBACBACBA, where C, B, and A are convolutional, batchnorm, and LeakyReLU layers, respectively. In each block, the first two convolutional layers have kernel size of 3, stride 1 and padding 1, while the last layer has kernel size of 2, padding 0 and stride 2. The first convolutional layer of the first block is not followed by a batchnorm layer. After the six blocks, we use a smaller block with CBA where the convolutional layer has kernel size 4, stride 1 and padding 0. The output of the last block is flattened and passed into two fully connected layers. Our models have between 10 and 30 million free parameters.

We train the networks for 200 epochs using the AdamW optimizer [18] with batch size equal to 128. We perform hyper-parameter optimization using the optuna package [19]. We train using data augmentation on the maps, rotations and flipping of the maps, to teach the model to preserve rotational and parity symmetries. We emphasize that by construction, our model is already invariant under translations. We provide further details on the architecture and training procedure in our companion paper [16].

The two networks are trained using either IllustrisTNG or SIMBA total mass maps from CAMELS simulations at $z=0$ . We then test the models using either IllustrisTNG or SIMBA maps from their test sets. We show the results for $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ in the left and right panels, respectively. The network is capable to recover the true value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ with high-accuracy in all situations, even when the network is tested on maps from simulations completely different to the ones used to train the model.*

We first train and validate a network using maps from 900 and 50 IllustrisTNG simulations, respectively. We test the model on maps from the 50 IllustrisTNG simulations of the test set (Fig. 2). We find that the model is able to infer the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ with high accuracy: $\langle\delta\Omega_{\rm m}/\Omega_{\rm m}\rangle\simeq 3.4\%$ , $\langle\delta\sigma_{8}/\sigma_{8}\rangle\simeq 2.4\%$ . The network can also infer the value of $A_{\rm SN1}$ and $A_{\rm SN2}$ but with much larger errors: $\langle\delta A_{\rm SN1}/A_{\rm SN1}\rangle\simeq 38\%$ and $\langle\delta A_{\rm SN1}/A_{\rm SN1}\rangle\simeq 17\%$ . On the other hand, the network is not capable of constraining the parameters controlling the efficiency of AGN feedback.

We now test the above model using maps from the SIMBA simulations. We emphasize that the above model has never seen a map from those simulations in the training. We show the results in Fig. 2 for a subset of 40 maps. Each point represents a map from the SIMBA simulations; the dot is the posterior mean while the errorbar shows the posterior standard deviation. We find that the network trained on the IllustrisTNG maps is able to infer the true value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ from the SIMBA maps with a similar accuracy to that for the IllustrisTNG maps: $\langle\delta\Omega_{\rm m}/\Omega_{\rm m}\rangle\simeq 3.9\%$ , $\langle\delta\sigma_{8}/\sigma_{8}\rangle\simeq 2.6\%$ . We emphasize that the SIMBA simulations not only solve the hydrodynamic equations in a different way than the IllustrisTNG simulations, but the subgrid model is also quite distinct. Thus, it is not obvious that this test should work at all. On the other hand, the network completely fails at predicting the astrophysical parameters. This is expected since the astrophysical parameters in the IllustrisTNG and SIMBA simulations are different in definition and in their effect on multiple quantities (see [10] for a detailed discussion).

Next, we train another network with the same architecture but using maps from the SIMBA simulations. As above, we employ maps from 900 and 50 simulations for training and validating the model. We first test the model using SIMBA maps from the test set. We find results very similar to those obtained when training and testing with IllustrisTNG maps: the network is able to infer the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ with high accuracy, $\langle\delta\Omega_{\rm m}/\Omega_{\rm m}\rangle\simeq 4.5\%$ , $\langle\delta\sigma_{8}/\sigma_{8}\rangle\simeq 2.7\%$ (see Fig. 2). The model can also put some constraints on $A_{\rm SN1}$ ( $49\%$ ) and $A_{\rm SN2}$ ( $23\%$ ), while the AGN parameters cannot be inferred. We note that the average errors on the value of the cosmological parameters from this network are slightly higher than those from the model trained on IllustrisTNG maps. This could be because the SIMBA simulations have a wider range of effective variation in the astrophysics parameters, which could force the network to marginalize more deeply than in the IllustrisTNG maps.

Finally, we test this model using IllustrisTNG maps. The results are very similar to those discussed above. Namely, we find that the model is able to accurately infer the value of the cosmological parameters: $\langle\delta\Omega_{\rm m}/\Omega_{\rm m}\rangle\simeq 4.3\%$ , $\langle\delta\sigma_{8}/\sigma_{8}\rangle\simeq 2.7\%$ . On the other hand, this model is unable to infer any value of the astrophysical parameters of these maps, as expected for the reasons discussed above.

These results illustrate how neural networks can 1) extract information from the field and 2) marginalize over baryonic effects. The most important point we would like to emphasize in this paper is that this procedure seems to be robust, i.e., it does not rely on training on a particular set of simulations with a particular hydrodynamics solver and implementation of subgrid physics. In our companion paper [9] we showed that this may not always be the case; when repeating the above exercise using gas temperature maps, the model is not robust.

We now carry out a set of tests as an attempt to understand what the network is doing and what it is not. First, we investigate whether the network is only using information from the total mass in the maps to do the inference. Since the total mass in a simulation is proportional to $\Omega_{\rm m}$ , we expect a certain degree of correlation between that parameter and the total mass of our maps. We first make a scatter plot between the total mass in a map and its value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ , and as expected we find a correlation with $\Omega_{\rm m}$ . However, it is not large enough to explain the few percent errors we obtain from the network. This occurs because our maps only represent volumes of $25\times 25\times 5~(h^{-1}{\rm Mpc})^{3}$ and so cosmic variance breaks the perfect correlation between $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and the total mass in a simulation box. Furthermore, with the network trained, we feed it with maps where all pixels contain the mean mass density per pixel. In this case, the network is not able to infer the value of any of the parameters. This shows that the network is not just using the total mass in a map to do the inference.

Next, we explore whether the network is performing inference via clustering or just through some 1-point function. To this end, we input maps where the pixel values are randomly shuffled into the network; if the network was just extracting information from, e.g., the probability distribution function, then the ordering of the pixels would not matter. We find that also in this case the network cannot perform parameter inference. This shows that the network is using information from the spatial distribution of the maps.

We also study whether the network is extracting more information than the traditional summary statistic used in cosmology: the power spectrum. For this purpose, we compute the power spectrum of all the maps and perform likelihood-free inference on it. We use fully connected layers and perform hyper-parameter optimization over the number of layers, number of neurons per layer, learning rate, weight decay, and dropout rate. We find that the information embedded in the power spectrum only suffices to infer the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ with very large error bars: $\langle\delta{\Omega}_{\rm m}/\Omega_{\rm m}\rangle\simeq 20\%$ . For the other five parameters the network only predicts the mean with large errorbars. This test shows that the network is extracting information beyond the power spectrum; that information beats the one in the power spectrum by a large margin.

One hypothesis that could explain our results is that the contamination from baryonic effects in the maps is negligible, so the network does not need to learn to marginalize over baryonic effects. This could also explain why training on one simulation type and testing on another works so well. To test this hypothesis, we train a neural network on maps from the CAMELS N-body simulations, which span the same range in $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ as their hydrodynamic counterparts. These simulations do not model baryonic effects, so the network does not need to marginalize over them. We input maps of the total mass from the hydrodynamic simulations into the network trained on the N-body maps. We find that the network fails to infer the value of the cosmological parameters. This clearly shows that our maps are sensitive to baryonic effects. This is completely expected, and we refer the reader to Fig. 7 of [10] for a plot showing the effect of baryons on the 3D matter power spectrum at $z=0$ .

One may wonder if the neural network is just marginalizing over baryonic effects by ignoring scales affected by them; one can achieve this by, e.g., convolving the maps with a filter that suppresses clustering below a given scale. If that was the case, then the network trained on total mass maps from hydrodynamic simulations would also work when testing on maps from N-body simulations. When we make this test we also find that the network cannot perform a good inference on the value of the cosmological parameters, showing that the network does not seem to be marginalizing over baryonic effects by ignoring small scales.

To demonstrate more clearly that the network is extracting cosmological information from all scales, we first smooth the total mass maps from the hydrodynamic simulations using a Gaussian kernel with different widths of one, two, and three pixels. We then retrain the model with these three types of maps. We find that these models are able to infer the value of the cosmological parameters, but the errorbars are larger; the larger the width of the Gaussian kernel, the larger the standard deviation of the posterior. This clearly indicates that the original network, trained on maps that were not smoothed, was extracting cosmological information from the smallest scales, $\sim 100~h^{-1}{\rm kpc}$ , the ones that are expected to be more heavily contaminated by baryonic effects. We provide further details on these tests in the supplemental material.

From these tests we can draw the following conclusions: 1) the network is not doing something trivial such as using the total mass in the maps or computing its 1-point PDF, but 2) the network is extracting information beyond the power spectrum on different scales, including the smallest scales sampled by our maps, while 3) the network is marginalizing over baryonic effects at the field level. More importantly, even if the methods used to solve the hydrodynamic equations in the IllustrisTNG and SIMBA simulations are very different, as are their subgrid models, one can train networks using one set of simulations that are able to marginalize over baryonic effects when testing on the other set. This shows how robust and powerful this method can potentially be.

We leave for future work a deeper and more complete analysis of what features and elements of the cosmic web the network is focusing its attention on in order to perform the inference. We will also investigate in more detail how the network marginalizes over baryonic effects and extracts cosmological information from the smallest scales sampled by our maps. It is important to understand why this method seems robust against astrophysics and how this information can be leveraged with real surveys.

We will also study how robust parameter inference is with other fields, like the ones we have explored in [9] such as gas mass, gas temperature, and electron density. We emphasize that the results reported in this work are probably lower bounds, as real data may be affected by systematics and noise, which will increase errors. On the other hand, our method is able to extract robust information from very small scales from fields that are highly non-linear, showing that it should be easier to apply this procedure to real data, where projections will Gaussianize weak lensing maps. On the other side, from the smoothing analysis above, we expect there would be significantly less information for the network to extract.

Our results have important implications for cosmology. For example, while the 2D total mass density projections we have considered in this paper are not directly observable, they can be seen as the lensing planes that ultimately give rise to weak gravitational lensing. Our framework opens the door to extracting information from such maps down to the smallest resolved scales, which are rich in information. Furthermore, we have shown that one can simulate baryonic effects using a particular method to solve the hydrodynamic equations and subgrid implementation, and as long as the range of variation is large enough, be robust to the exact scheme employed. Overall, this work illustrates the potential of applying deep learning to optimally tackle parameter estimation in cosmology from upcoming multi-wavelength surveys.

Supplemental Material

Here we provide further details on some of the tests carried out that due to space limitations were only briefly described in the main text.

Baryonic effects. As discussed in the main text, one of the potential explanations of our results is that the maps we are considering have a negligible contamination by baryonic effects. Thus, it does not really matter whether they are produced from IllustrisTNG or SIMBA simulations, and a network trained on one should work on the other. If that would be the case, we could train a neural network on maps from the N-body simulations, that are not contaminated by baryonic effects and then test it on maps from either IllustrisTNG or SIMBA. The left panel of Fig. 3 shows the results of training a network on maps from the N-body simulations and testing them on total matter mass density from the IllustrisTNG simulations. As can be seen, the network is not able to infer the value of neither $\Omega_{\rm m}$ nor $\sigma_{8}$ . It is however interesting to observe that in the case of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ , the network is almost working; the prediction exhibits a bias that gets larger with higher values of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ . We do not attempt to explain these results here.

Cutoff scale. In cosmological analyses it is a standard practice to apply a cutoff in scale in order to avoid uncertainties in non-linear scales as well as baryonic effects. We may wonder if our network is doing something similar, i.e. extracting information from scales not affected by baryonic effects while neglecting all information from scales affected by astrophysics. If that would be the case, we would expect that a network trained on maps from the hydrodynamic simulations would be able to infer the value of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_{8}$ from maps from N-body simulations. We have carried out this test and show the results in the right panel of Fig. 3. As can be seen, also in this case the network is not able to infer the value of the cosmological parameters from the N-body maps. It is also very interesting to note that the prediction of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ seems to be off by a constant factor. We believe this offset has some physical implications, although we do not attempt to provide an explanation in this work. For $\sigma_{8}$ instead, we find that the prediction is worse for lower values of $\Omega_{\rm m}$ ; we found a similar behavior in the test mentioned above.

*Figure 3: Left: We have trained a neural network using maps from N-body simulations and tested the model on maps from the total matter mass density of IllustrisTNG simulations. Right: We have tested the model that was trained on total matter mass density maps from IllustrisTNG simulations on N-body maps. As can be seen, neither test worked, indicating that 1) the reason why the networks perform so well cannot be that maps are barely affected by baryonic effects and 2) the network is not applying a cut on the scales affected by baryonic effects.*

*Figure 4: We have trained four neural networks on IllustrisTNG maps with no smoothing (red) and smoothing the maps with a Gaussian kernel of size 1 pixel (green), 2 pixels (magenta), and 3 pixels (blue). This figure shows the results when testing these networks on IllustrisTNG maps with the same characteristic as those used in their training. The average relative accuracy, $\langle\sigma_{i}/\mu_{i}\rangle$ , is displayed in the upper part of the plot. As can be seen, by smoothing the maps, the network is only able to infer the value of the cosmological parameters with lower accuracy. This indicates that the network trained on the maps that are not smoothed is extracting information from the smallest scales (1 pixel) available in the map.*

Smoothing test. In order to investigate on which scales the network is extracting information, we have taken the IllustrisTNG maps and smooth them with a Gaussian kernel of width equal to 1 pixel, 2 pixels, and 3 pixels. Those maps are then used to train three different neural networks. In Fig. 4 we show the results. As can be seen, the larger the width of the Gaussian kernel, the less information the network is able to extract. The average relative accuracy on $\Omega_{\rm m}$ degrades from 3.4% in the case of no smooth to 5.1% (1 pixel), 6.8% (2 pixels), and 8.8% (3 pixels); for $\sigma_{8}$ it changes from 2.4% in the case of no smoothing to 2.7% (1 pixel), 3.2% (2 pixels), and 3.7% (3 pixels). These results indicate that the original network is extracting cosmological information from the smallest scales resolved in our maps, i.e. at the pixel level. Besides, this also suggest that more information can be extracted from higher resolution maps.

tructural injustice remains a puzzling concept despite its increasing prominence. I distill recent theoretical challenges into a dilemma: either structural injustice lacks the normative credentials of injustice given that wrongdoing is inessential, or it is redundant given existing theories that trace injustice to culpable state and other institutional failures. I thendevelop a novel account of structural injustice, the Complexity View, that unravels this dilemma. The emergent properties of human actions in a complex society explain what is “structural” about structural injustice, specifically how it can arise without (culpable) wrongdoing. Structural injustice is unjust because it is wrong to contribute to social processes that cause harm and to passively accept preventable forms of vulnerability and deprivation as tragic misfortunes. But this account of structural injustice has a sobering implication: while complexity explains what distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, it also sets significant epistemic limits on social reform.

INTRODUCTION S

tructural injustice has become a prominent topic in contemporary political theory. In contrast to wrongs found in interpersonal interactions or the policies of a repressive state, Iris Marion Young (2011) argues in her pathbreaking account, structural injustice is a wrong that lies in the cumulative constraining and enabling effects of social structures in the backdrop of people’s lives, effects that significantly harm certain groups. These effects, she argues, are produced by complex social processes driven by the actions, not necessarily wrongful, of many people pursuing legitimate goals within the existing framework of rules and resources. By broadening our normative focus from individual and institutional wrongdoings toward unjust yet often ignored forms of vulnerability and deprivation within our social structures, the concept of structural injustice aims to illuminate a distinctive and pressing problem in contemporary society for social criticism and political redress. Yet the concept of structural injustice continues to generate theoretical puzzlement and disagreement. Two recent criticisms of Young’s account bring out one important puzzle. For some critics, we should be skeptical that these sorts of problems count as an injustice in the first place. Plausibly, what distinguishes injustice from mere tragedy or misfortune is its origin in the wrongful conduct of human agents, conduct that warrants moral grievances like anger or indignation (Estlund 2024). It is unclear whether something that occurs without any wrongdoing has the normative credentials of injustice. Thus, these critics ask, if structural injustice is not necessarily the result of anyone

doing anything wrong, why should our attitude toward it be any different than our attitude toward natural disasters and their terrible, but not wrongful, effects? The question is not specific to the concept of structural injustice but applies more broadly to cognates ideas like structural racism as “racism without racists” (Bonilla- Silva 2003) or capitalism as an inherently unjust economic structure (Cordelli 2025). Any structural theory of injustice must answer the question: given that wrongdoing is inessential, what’s unjust about structural injustice? Other critics have questioned the purported distinction between structural injustice and institutional wrongdoing. A wave of recent accounts argues that institutional wrongdoing plays a central role in structural injustice (Mantouvalou 2023; McKeown 2024; Nuti 2019; Powers and Faden 2019). According to Maeve McKeown, Young mistakenly focused on conceptualizing “pure” structural injustice involving no wrongdoing whatsoever. In reality, most if not all structural injustices are “deliberate” or “avoidable” wrongs perpetrated by the powerful institutional agents like the state. Homelessness, McKeown (2024, 41–2) argues about one of Young’s core examples, can and should be addressed by the state through measures like implementing rent control and building more public housing; that affluent states have largely failed to do so is a serious wrongdoing on their part. Far from being conceptually distinct from institutional wrongdoing, these accounts argue, structural injustice is a problem perpetrated largely by the wrongdoings of powerful institutions. Together, these criticisms reveal a significant tension within the concept of structural injustice. As a claim of injustice, it looks normatively suspect unless it can be tethered to agential wrongdoing. Pointing to institutional wrongdoing, as recent accounts do, would seem to dispel such suspicions. To put this point more sharply, once institutions like states and corporations are understood to be agents in their own right (List and Pettit 2011), the concept of structural injustice appears redundant: there already exist theories of justice and injustice that trace injustices in contemporary society to institutions like the state as powerful agents that wield enormous influence over social outcomes, and it is unclear what, if anything, the concept of structural injustice adds to these theories. Some may welcome this deflationary conclusion. But the thought that the concept of structural injustice names a distinct problem in contemporary society from both individual and institutional wrongdoing remains attractive to many, even as its theoretical difficulties have become increasingly clear. This article develops a novel account of what structural injustice is and why it is unjust, and in doing so, offers a solution to this puzzle. I call this account the Complexity View. What is distinctively “structural” about structural injustice is its basis in the emergent properties of human actions in society, understood as a kind of complex system. Many harmful social outcomes are not straightforwardly reducible to or predictable from features of the agents who bring them about; indeed, these outcomes often run contrary to what any of those agents intended. This counterintuitive relationship between action and outcome in a complex society explains how structural injustice comes apart from wrongdoing (or at least culpable wrongdoing) and why it cannot be chalked up to faulty institutions. What is unjust about structural injustice is explained by two moral considerations: the wrongfulness of agents causing harm to others even when that harm was unintended and unforeseeable, and the wrongfulness of agents passively resigning themselves to harmful emergent outcomes that are preventable through political intervention and social reform. In these ways, structural injustice has the normative credentials of injustice. If successful, the Complexity View shows that the concept of structural injustice is both plausible and valuable. It illuminates how human actions can create emergent forms of vulnerability and deprivation in a complex society, while also issuing a reminder that these problems are neither natural disasters nor invulnerable to political redress. That said, this account comes with a sobering implication for how agents can and should politically respond to these problems: the very same issue of complexity that essentially distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs also creates significant, though surmountable, epistemic barriers for the pursuit of deliberate and effective social reform.

THE DILEMMA FOR STRUCTURAL INJUSTICE

To begin making the central puzzle more concrete, consider a widely discussed example from Young (2011, 43–4): the case of Sandy, a single mother and commuter in a typical American city who ends up facing homelessness when her current apartment

building is sold to a developer, setting off a chain of events in which various structural constraints produced by the actions of countless others—from the price and availability of housing in her city to the quality of schools in different neighborhoods—prevent her from finding a new residence, leaving her on the verge of homelessness. As Young sets up the case, no one treats Sandy wrongly during this ordeal. Nonetheless, Sandy finds herself facing a common and, Young argues, unjust situation. It is unjust that anyone should face the prospect of homelessness, especially in an affluent society. Sandy experiences a structural injustice, and this is a distinct phenomenon from agential wrongdoing. Many have found Young’s description of Sandy’s situation compelling. Others have different reactions. One is that Sandy’s situation is surely the product of at least one (collective) agent’s wrongdoing: her state. Her state should be doing more to ensure that Sandy and others like her are not vulnerable to homelessness; it bears responsibility for her situation. Another is that Sandy’s situation is not an injustice, however unfortunate it may be, given that it is not the result of anyone having wronged her in any way. Of course, she is entitled to some help to get back on her feet—but that is a matter of human decency or charity, not a matter of her having suffered an injustice. These reactions correspond to what I call the redundancy challenge and the normative challenge, respectively. The redundancy challenge says the concept of structural injustice is unnecessary: everything we want to say with the concept of structural injustice can and should be said in terms of individual and collective wrongdoings. The normative challenge says the concept of structural injustice is implausible: to the extent that it is essentially about something other than agential wrongdoing, it lacks the normative credentials to be an injustice. Despite their important insights, existing accounts of structural injustice are vulnerable to at least one of these challenges. Young’s account is vulnerable to the normative challenge. She maintains that structural injustice is distinct from individual and institutional wrongdoing, but she does not offer an alternative explanation of why it is unjust and not merely tragic. Situations like Sandy’s, she suggests, are obviously unjust. But this is not a satisfactory answer to the normative challenge, as David Estlund (2024) has recently argued. For any situation that seems obviously unjust, he asks, suppose that the exact same situation had been produced by an unpreventable natural disaster like a hurricane. Such occurrences are commonly considered tragedies, not injustices. The relevant difference between the two is a moral, specifically a deontic, fact: unpreventable natural disasters are not a matter of anyone having treated others wrongly, indeed not a matter of human action at all.1 What plausibly

Recent accounts of structural injustice appear less vulnerable to the normative challenge (Mantouvalou 2023; McKeown 2024; Nuti 2019; Powers and Faden 2019). Departing from Young, they argue that structural injustice is, at least in large part, the product of wrongdoings by the state and other powerful collective or corporate agents. In McKeown’s (2024, 181 and 44) words, “powerful corporate agents like states and corporations can be held morally responsible for structural injustice, either by omission (avoidable structural injustice) or action (deliberate structural injustice)” because “powerful agents have the capacity to change the situation, [but] they actively maintain it. So the consequences are not unintentional, they are intentional.” Sandy would not be facing homelessness if her state took action, such as improving tenants’ rights and implementing rent control. By failing to implement such measures now and in the past, her state bears responsibility for her situation. Once the role of these powerful collective agents is acknowledged, the claim that structural injustice is distinct from wrongdoing looks less plausible and, in any case, irrelevant to understanding injustices here and now. Importantly, these accounts do not completely part ways with Young’s account. They maintain that individuals are not culpable for their part in structural injustice, because the conduct of ordinary individuals is not “where the action is, both in terms of understanding structural stability or change and in attributing responsibility for structural injustice” (McKeown 2024, 36–7). Structural injustice is primarily the product of wrongful institutional conduct. Call this the Institutional View of structural injustice. The Institutional View seems to offer a straightforward answer to the normative challenge: structural injustice is unjust because it is traceable to the wrongful conduct of powerful collective agents. Sandy’s situation is not a tragedy; it is a deliberate or avoidable injustice perpetrated by her state, real estate corporations, and other powerful institutions. A closer examination, however, reveals some problems with this answer. The trouble lies in the Institutional View’s ambiguous stance on whether structural injustice is simply a product of collective agents’ wrongdoing or whether it is in fact the product of a much broader and complicated set of human actions involving, crucially, ordinary individuals. Is structural injustice ultimately the product of collective agents’ wrongdoings, or is it only largely the product of such wrongdoings (and if so, how large)?

Take patriarchy as an example. Estlund (2024, 353) writes, “The many instances of individual behavior that together produce a patriarchal social structure…are, in large part even if not entirely, acts that are uncoordinated across strangers.” Here he challenges, rightly, the Institutional View’s claim that the conduct of ordinary individuals is not “where the action is” for structural injustice. Social structures like patriarchy are not just what powerful institutions do. Sharon Krause (2013, 194) recounts a memorable example of how social processes like gender socialization among individuals play an important role in patriarchy’s reproduction: “When I was a girl my mother was constantly enjoining me to ‘take smaller steps’ so as to be more ‘ladylike’. Apparently, my natural stride was too long, perhaps too forceful, to be feminine….[H]er exhortations, intended as loving guidance, did have the effect of socializing me to norms that subtly perpetuate inequalities between men and women.” Pointing to group agents thus offers only a partial answer to the normative challenge. To establish the deontic wrongness of structural injustice, the actions of many other agents must be normatively accounted for. Defenders of the Institutional View could respond in two ways. One response is to move further away from Young’s account and say that ordinary individuals, not just states and corporations, are guilty of wrongdoing when their actions contribute to structural injustice.2 This would provide a full answer to the normative challenge. But this move is not available to the Institutional View given its central commitment to the uniquely wrongful role of powerful institutions for problems of structural injustice. More importantly, to say that individuals are also guilty for contributing to structural injustice and simply leaving the matter there would be to miss one of the important points of Krause’s example. Ordinary individuals do contribute to structural injustices like patriarchy, but the nature of their contribution is not always something that licenses guilt or blame. Krause (2013, 195) writes, “The truth is that we participate all the time in practices that subordinate us even as they perpetuate the domination of others, and much of the time these acts of subordination and domination are neither recognized as such nor intended, much less controlled.” Socializing one’s child into certain gender norms is now seen by many as wrongful: as Krause’s own reflections demonstrate, people have come to understand that this practice perpetuates gender inequality and stifles individual freedom. This understanding may have innocently eluded Krause’s mother who, Krause observes, was well intentioned and in many ways a victim of patriarchy herself. But now the redundancy challenge rears its head. The Institutional View, so understood, threatens to make the concept of structural injustice theoretically redundant, or at least significantly deflates what appeared interesting and distinctive about it. Much work in political theory has already argued for the view that social injustices are rooted in powerful institutions like the state and their profound and pervasive influence on people’s lives, what John Rawls (1999) calls the “basic structure of society.” If structural injustice should be understood as a deliberate or avoidable wrong committed by powerful institutions, is it not just a species of institutional wrongdoing after all? What is gained, theoretically or politically, by calling Sandy’s situation a structural injustice rather than an institutional failure if the problem simply lies in her state’s unjust housing policies? The same can be asked about other issues like global poverty, which McKeown (2024, 102) claims is an avoidable structural injustice because “international institutions and powerful states have the capacity to change the structures that underlie global poverty”—a familiar argument in the literature on global (distributive) justice (see, e.g., Pogge 2002). The Institutional View has the resources to fully answer the normative challenge, but in doing so, it collapses structural injustice into the familiar question of institutional justice (Browne 2025, 31; De Bernardi 2024). Some may argue that this is exactly the right way to think about structural injustice and what is “structural” about it. Social structure, in their view, is fundamentally about institutional design, how “the rules of the game in a society” (North 1990, 3) set by institutions like the state channel human interactions in a certain direction. But there are plausible views in social and political

theory that maintain that the idea of social structure encompasses much more than institutional rules. Indeed, for Young, that is precisely the point of conceptualizing structural injustice. Drawing on insights from social theorists such as Pierre Bourdieu (1977) and Anthony Giddens (1984), she insists that the concept identifies a phenomenon that is generally overlooked by theories of justice that analyze social structure by examining the state and other formal institutions. Taking a truly structural perspective on injustice requires “looking at the whole society” and the social processes driven by the actions of all agents within it, not just looking at a small institutional subset of that society that is assumed to be “more fundamental” (or more powerful) than the rest (Young 2011, 70).3 Examples of such processes include the normalization of a dominant racial or ethnic group’s cultural values and habits, the reproduction of the gendered division of labor in households, and, as Krause reminds us, the transmission of gendered bodily comportment to children. Undoubtedly, these processes are significantly influenced by what institutions do. But it would be a serious mistake to assume that these social processes can simply be placed under institutional control or that the individual behaviors driving these processes can be read off from the institutional framework of rules in which they occur, absent further facts about culture, norms, bodies, etc. To my eye, this broader understanding of social structure is crucial for a nonredundant conceptualization of structural injustice. It is what makes the concept novel and interesting, theoretically and politically. The trouble with the Institutional View is that it gives up this important insight in its understandable quest to hold powerful institutions morally responsible for structural injustice. It claims, or must claim in response to the normative challenge, that certain institutions are the more powerful, fundamental part of society—“where the action is”—to maintain that structural injustice is the result of wrongful institutional conduct while ignoring the actions of ordinary individuals and exempting them from similar moral evaluation. The theoretical cost of this move is to make the concept of structural injustice redundant. Any so-called structural injustice could be fully redescribed in terms of institutional wrongdoing. At best, the concept of structural injustice would serve as a stepping stone for filling some overlooked gap in the theory of institutional justice, but once that theory is filled out, it would say everything the concept was meant to capture. Together, these challenges pose a dilemma for the concept of structural injustice. The more that structural injustice is untethered from agential wrongdoing, the less it looks like a genuine injustice, rather than a tragedy that is morally indistinct from a natural disaster. EMERGENCE, COMPLEXITY, AND SPONTANEOUS ORDER

This section begins developing an account of structural injustice that unravels this puzzle, building on Young’s important but underdeveloped thought that structural injustice is a product of complex social processes driven, in large part, by ordinary individuals and their actions. A major step toward this account is taken in Sally Haslanger’s (2022; 2023) recent work in social ontology, which integrates ideas from social theory and philosophy into an original theory of society as a complex dynamic system structured by the social practices of individuals. One notable passage reads: “Societies are not planned and implemented by anyone. They are self-organizing systems. Although legislatures, economists, planning boards, and policy makers undertake to construct and intervene in social systems, and what they do matters, they are not in control. The society, so to speak, has a life of its own, and much of what happens is not designed or intended by anyone” (Haslanger 2023, 9). This is a strikingly different picture of society from the Institutional View. Here, the state (and other powerful institutions) is but one agent among many in the system, and as comparatively powerful as it may be, it is not “in control” of the society it aims to manage. Why not? Consider the issue of racial residential segregation, “the linchpin” (Massey 2020) of racial inequality in the United States as a problem of structural injustice. It is now widely recognized that ending legally enforced or de jure segregation has not addressed de facto segregation: a recent study finds that most metropolitan areas were more racially segregated in 2019 than they were in 1990 (Menendian, Gambhir, and Gailes 2021). Part of the explanation for this is a history of culpable discriminatory practices by political, financial, and real estate institutions, such as redlining, that have only recently been outlawed. But it would be a mistake to attribute the persistence of residential segregation to institutional actors alone. Residential segregation is also driven by social processes that the state does not control, most notably the choices of many individuals navigating the housing market. Thus, Elizabeth Anderson (2010b, 189) closes her book-length argument for racial integration as an imperative of justice with the sobering observation that “the project of integration cannot be left to state initiatives alone. Most of the work of integration inevitably rests with the spontaneous

actions of citizens in civil society.”4 Notice again the gap between this picture and the Institutional View. Contrary to the Institutionalist View’s claim that powerful institutions like the state are “where the action is,” here state action cannot succeed unless ordinary individuals take the necessary actions and develop the necessary attitudes and habits for a truly, not just formally, integrated society (Anderson 2010b, 116). It is tempting to conclude from these considerations that ordinary individuals must also be culpable for their part in structural injustice. Regarding residential segregation, it may be argued that responding to the racial diversification of one’s neighborhood by moving to white enclaves or “white flight” is a culpable behavior for which white individuals bear some responsibility for racial inequality (Kruse 2007). What ordinary individuals do within the remit of their everyday lives is socially consequential, and they should be held responsible for their actions. But the issue is not so straightforward, and this is where the gap between structural injustice and agential wrongdoing begins to appear. Racial hostility is not required for segregated neighborhoods to result from individual residential choices. As Thomas Schelling (1969; 1971) famously demonstrated, segregated neighborhoods can form even when agents navigate a housing market with a preference that at least roughly one out of three neighbors belong to their own racial group, a result that intensifies when the preference is raised to one-half.5 In other words, individuals who are perfectly content to be the racial minority in their neighborhood by a ratio of 2-to-1 end up forming segregated neighborhoods. Racial residential segregation, in principle, need not involve culpable actions like redlining and white flight; surprisingly, it can be the product of many agents acting on what intuitively appear to be innocuous in-group preferences about their neighborhood. The housing market, Schelling (1969, 488) concludes, is “a complex system with collective results that bear no close relation to individual intent.” And as Joseph Heath (2022, 299) observes, if collective results and individual intentions come apart, then “it becomes impossible to say anything about the relative levels of discrimination or tolerance merely from observing the spatial distribution of individuals of different races.” We cannot infer culpable attitudes or actions toward other racial groups from the occurrence of segregation alone. In a complex system, the actions of many agents create emergent properties that are not simply reducible to the properties of the agents that create them. These properties are what license Haslanger’s claim that “society has, so to speak, a life of its own,” thus presenting a distinct object of study—and critique— from the individuals and institutions that comprise it. The basic idea of emergence, often associated with the phrase “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts,” is an old one. Émile Durkheim ([1895] 2013) invoked it to justify social science as a distinctive field of study: society exhibits empirically investigable properties that are not reducible to properties of individuals even though society contains nothing but individuals. But emergence is not specific to sociology. Challenging the purported hierarchy in the natural sciences from (fundamental) physics to (more applied) biology, P. W. Anderson (1972, 393) writes: “The behavior of large and complex aggregates of elementary particles, it turns out, is not to be understood in terms of a simple extrapolation of the properties of a few particles. Instead, at each level of complexity entirely new properties appear.” The concept of structural injustice is premised on a similar claim: the interactions of human agents in a complex society create emergent properties, properties that are not simply reducible to the properties of individuals themselves. While familiar, the basic idea of emergence requires elaboration, for it can be given more and less plausible interpretations. Recent years have seen a proliferation of philosophical accounts of emergence that respond to longstanding worries about its metaphysical and scientific plausibility. For my purposes, it is important to distinguish between two varieties of emergence: ontological emergence and epistemic emergence.6 Each offers a different gloss of the claim that an emergent property of a system is not simply reducible to the properties of its constituent parts. In ontological emergence, an emergent property is metaphysically distinct from its constituent lower-level properties because there are reasons to hold that the property exists in its own right. Such reasons include causal novelty (the emergent property can cause some effect, and this ability is different from even the aggregated causal powers of the lower-level properties) or non-deducibility (the emergent property is not deducible from the lower-level properties even if one knew everything about them). So understood, emergence is heavily criticized for creating more mysteries than it solves: how can something be generated entirely by

lower-level properties, and yet have novel causal powers or be non-deducible from those properties? (Kim 1999). Some deny on these grounds that there are any ontologically emergent properties, pointing to successful reductionist explanations of properties that formerly were considered emergent in the history of science (Graham 2025). Others, such as David Chalmers (2008), argue that there is exactly one plausible instance of ontological emergence: consciousness, as a property not deducible even from complete knowledge of the physical properties of the brain. These criticisms apply to the issue of residential segregation. It seems implausible to say that residential segregation is an ontologically emergent property. Indeed, Schelling’s model shows precisely the deducibility of segregated neighborhoods from the preferences of agents making choices under certain conditions, though the relationship between the individuals and the emergent property is surprising and far from straightforward. That brings us to epistemic emergence. Following Mark Bedau (1997), a property is epistemically emergent insofar as it is deducible from its lower-level properties only by simulation: “set up the system, let it roll, and see what happens.”7 Simulation is required because although the emergent property is fully determined by its lower-level properties, how those lowerlevel properties interact to produce the emergent property is too complex a process to be predictable from knowledge of the lower-level properties. In Schelling’s model, agents following the simple decision rule “Move into a house so long as at least roughly 1/3 of the neighbors are members of my racial group” end up forming segregated neighborhoods, a result that only becomes apparent to us by simulating its implementation. In this epistemic sense, this result is not simply reducible to the actions or intentions of the agents, even if it is their actions and intentions that produced it. The process by which residential segregation is generated by agents’ choices is not explicable by the linear cause-andeffect reasoning that typically suffices in everyday life. My contention is that the kinds of outcomes that plausibly count as structural injustice are epistemically emergent. The concept of structural injustice invites us to look at society as a kind of complex system where multiple overlapping social processes, driven by many agents engaged in economic, cultural, linguistic, and other interactions, produce some vulnerability or deprivation as their emergent outcome. Some social processes, such as economic interactions in a market, are themselves a kind of complex system that produces emergent outcomes—a fact that puts considerable stress on domestically oriented theories of economic justice as well as conceptions of “society” as a closed, self-contained nation-state in an era of globalization. When they have harmful effects on human lives, such outcomes can be described as structural injustice. Such outcomes include racial disparities in infant mortality (Wallace et al. 2017), economic inequalities perpetuated by people’s accents (Donnelly, Baratta, and Gamsu 2019), and colonial atrocities like sexual slavery that end up disproportionately impacting poor women (Lu 2017, 128–38). These outcomes are, by nature, not linearly related to or straightforwardly predictable from the actions or intentions of the agents who bring them about. Indeed, the outcome may depart dramatically from what any agent intended or foresaw or could have foreseen. So understood, structural injustice presents a distinct problem from familiar kinds of wrongful individual and institutional actions like exiting a neighborhood out of racial prejudice or depriving a racial minority of equal political status. Such wrongdoings are routinely part of the processes that generate structural injustice, but they will not fully explain the emergent outcome. Indeed, focusing on such wrongdoings would obscure the fact that the outcome can arise without them, as when individuals with integrationist preferences still produce residential segregation. This is true even if wrongdoing is stretched beyond the intentional infliction of harm to the negligent failure to avoid foreseeably causing harm to others, since social interactions may produce emergent outcomes that were unforeseeable to the agents who produced it. In a complex system, it is possible for social interactions to produce vulnerability or deprivation without any agents having acted wrongly. It is this possibility that is foregrounded in Young and Haslanger’s accounts of structural injustice. Notably, Rawls also recognizes this possibility in his discussion of “background justice.” Social processes driven by the actions of ordinary individuals can have inimical results even within a just society: “the conditions necessary for background justice can be undermined, even though nobody acts unfairly or is aware of how the overall results of many separate exchanges affects the opportunities of others” (Rawls 1993, 266). The next line is crucial for understanding Rawls’ point: “There are no feasible rules that it is practicable to require economic agents to follow in their day-to-day transactions that can prevent these undesirable consequences.” In principle, he suggests here, there might be individual-level rules of economic interaction that would fully preserve background justice. But such rules are not relevant in practice due to the epistemically emergent nature of economic outcomes in a market economy: “the rules governing agreements and individual transactions cannot be too complex, or require too much information to be correctly applied” (Rawls 1993, 267). A society’s institutions may conform with Rawlsian principles of justice, but the justice they aim to uphold can erode over time from individual actions that are permitted in those institutions. In short, structural injustice is, at heart, a problem of complexity. This conceptualization of structural injustice bears a strong resemblance to F.A. Hayek’s notion of “spontaneous order,” at least in its ontological and epistemic claims (Hayek 1945; 1967; 1973; 1976; 1979). Hayek himself would deny that emergent social outcomes count as an injustice, as I will discuss in the next

section. While neither Young nor Haslanger reference Hayek’s work, their understanding of structural injustice similarly describes “the result of human actions but not the execution of any human design” (Ferguson 1767, 187). Hayek emphasized the unintended benefits of a market economy as opposed to a planned economy, but complex social processes do not only exist in the market, nor do these processes only produce unintended benefits.8 Playing on “spontaneous order,” structural injustice is an emergent disorder in a complex society.9 Call this the Complexity View. The Complexity View avoids the redundancy challenge: structural injustice does not simply collapse into agential wrongdoing, whether by individuals or institutions. The concept names a distinctive social phenomenon. Before turning to the normative challenge, let me address a potential worry about this view, namely that it is premised on a controversial social ontology involving mysterious “emergent” properties. To the extent that structural injustice can be conceptualized without it, one might argue, the better. That might be true. But it is not a point in favor of the Institutional View. A crucial assumption of that view is that the state and multinational corporations are themselves (collective) agents distinct from the (individual) agents that make them up. Following Christian List and Philip Pettit’s (2011) influential account, the Institutional View claims that collectives or groups are agents when and because they possess the constitutive capacities of agency due to their internal organization and procedures. But group agency itself, it turns out, is an emergent property in the epistemic sense. List and Pettit (2011, 76) write, “While the agency achieved by a group supervenes on the contributions of its members —while it is not ontologically autonomous—it is autonomous in another, related sense. The agency of the group relates in such a complex way to the agency of individuals that we have little chance of tracking the dispositions of the group agent, and of interacting with it as an agent to contest or interrogate, persuade or coerce, if we conceptualize its doings at the individual level.” Although they frame the issues in terms of supervenience and autonomy, the substantive point is that group agency is an epistemically emergent property of a group of individuals organized in a certain way. The Institutional View, then, rests on the acceptance of one particularly striking case of epistemic emergence: group agency. The idea of emergent properties is thus no more mysterious than the idea of treating the state and other institutions as agents in their own right.

An important feature of emergence in the context of social structures is that, ultimately, it is all a product of human agency. As agents, our knowledge of the emergent properties of our actions and our ability to intervene in society in response to them are not static and immutable facts but things that can change and develop over time. The fact that society contains epistemically emergent properties does not make impossible for agents to investigate and intervene in such phenomena as they become known— though it does impose significant limits on how agents can and should engage in such social reform, as the next section will explain. History contains many examples of agents collectively learning to navigate the emergent problems created by their social practices, such as the multiple revisions that economic theory and policy has undergone in the last 100 years in response to various economic crises (Widmaier 2016). Giddens (1990, 38) calls this process of social learning reflexivity: “social practices are constantly examined and reformed in the light of incoming information about those very practices, thus constitutively altering their character.”10 These reforms, he notes, often produce new emergent problems that we could not have foreseen in implementing these new practices, thereby generating new information and starting the cycle anew.11

Agency, understood not as the capacity to prospectively predict and avoid the emergent properties of human action but as the capacity to reflexively examine and respond to them as they arise, is the key to answering the normative challenge. Changes to what we know and can do about an emergent social problem also changes our moral relationship to that problem. In a

complex society, we should expect such changes to be a frequent occurrence. As Seyla Benhabib (2004, 104) observes in the context of burgeoning problems of global justice, “we are constantly being challenged in understanding the moral implications of our actions by discovering unintended consequences…Such knowledge creates moral responsibility.” I argue that there are two plausible and compatible, though independent, explanations of how deontic wrongness is created this way. Hayek overlooks these sources of deontic wrongness. Young also seems to overlook them, leading her to draw an immutable and thus untenable distinction between structural injustice and agential wrongdoing.12

One explanation is what I call the argument from contribution, which builds on some proposals by critics of Young’s distinction between structural injustice and individual wrongdoing (Atenasio 2019; Barry and Ferracioli 2013; Goodin and Barry 2021; Reiman 2012; Sangiovanni 2018). In their view, actions that contribute to producing structural injustice is a form of wrongdoing. This follows from the general principle that one ought not cause, or in collective action cases be part of the cause of, harm to others. There is a difference, however, between acting wrongly and acting culpably. Wrongful actions can be excused and not culpable when performed under certain conditions, including, notably, out of (reasonable) ignorance of their consequences. Those actions are no longer excused and become culpable, however, once this ignorance is dispelled (or is now itself culpable). Combining this with the earlier discussion of epistemic emergence and reflexivity gives us the following picture. Agents are not culpable for producing an emergent outcome, at first. They are excused by their ignorance. But the moral situation begins to change once the harmful outcome has been produced and people are suffering. Claiming ignorance of the harm produced by their social practices becomes increasingly an untenable excuse. The critical mistake in Young’s account is failing to distinguish culpability from wrongdoing: structural injustice that involves no culpable wrongdoing is possible in a complex society, but it is not a permanent condition for agents with the capacity to examine and re-evaluate their social practices in response to emergent problems. This objection raises an important question about collectively produced harms: if the actions of many individuals collectively produce a harm, yet no individual’s action considered on its own makes a difference to that harm, then what, if anything, makes those actions morally wrong? The other explanation of structural injustice’s normative credentials is what I call the argument from passive injustice, building on Judith Shklar’s (1990) influential discussion. Shklar contends that it is a mistake to think that whether something is an injustice depends only on its causal story, such that harmful outcomes that did not originate in wrongful conduct or “active injustice,” including natural disasters, must therefore be mere misfortunes. Equally important is the question of whether agents organized in a political community have the capacity to prevent or mitigate that harmful outcome. Where the capacity exists, it is “passive injustice” for the community to simply let the outcome happen, to be indifferent toward the vulnerable.16 Passive injustice applies to natural and social outcomes alike. Indeed, the fact that humans have repeatedly developed new ways of altering their natural environment should lead us to question the very distinction between what is natural and what is social, and with it, what is inevitable and what is contingent. As she observes, “[s]ome misfortunes of the past…are now injustices, such as infant mortality and famines” (Shklar 1990, 5). SOCIAL REFORM IN A COMPLEX SOCIETY

Recent theoretical challenges, I have argued, pose a dilemma for the concept of structural injustice: either it is distinct from agential wrongdoing but then lacks the normative credentials of injustice, or it is primarily a matter of institutional wrongdoing but then is theoretically redundant. The Complexity View offers a way out. Structural injustice is distinct from (culpable) wrongdoing because predicting the emergent outcomes of human actions is too epistemically difficult, such that structural injustice is not simply a product of (culpable) wrongdoing even though it is ultimately a product of human action. However, structural injustice as emergent disorder is unjust, not merely bad, because we are reflexive agents with the capacity to examine and reform our social practices in light of new information about their effects. Two forms of wrongdoing explain the wrongness of structural injustice: contributing to social processes that harm others, and failing to prevent or mitigate bad outcomes that are socially preventable or mitigable. So understood, structural injustice is a normatively plausible and theoretically valuable concept, one that identifies a distinctive social phenomenon for criticism and redress. One important but easily overlooked implication of this view, however, is that the pursuit of social reform itself faces epistemic limitations in a complex society.23 I will conclude by dwelling on this implication. Goodin and Barry (2021, 343) point out that the very same complexity that distinguishes structural injustice from agential wrongdoing may also threaten the justifiability of holding agents responsible for failing to remedy structural injustice. Structural injustice arises as an unintended consequence of what agents do, but the issue of unintended consequences does not magically disappear when agents introduce social reforms to try to address them. Their key contention and insight is that deliberate and effective social reform is possible even in a complex society so long as agents can imagine and try out alternative social arrangements in response to newfound social problems, learn from their experiences of living with those arrangements, and collectively decide whether the results are sufficiently positive to make those arrangements worth keeping and emulating. Elizabeth Anderson (2006, 13) writes in her explication of pragmatism: “Unfavorable results—failures to solve the problem for which the policy was adopted, or solving the problem but at the cost of generating worse problems—should be treated in a scientific spirit as disconfirmations of our policies.” But if we are not adept at predicting whether a reform will generate “worse problems,” some will argue, then perhaps it is better not to take the leap at all. Perhaps passivity in the face of structural injustice is not morally wrong but a reasonable response to the potential consequences of intervening in a complex society under deep uncertainty. But this conservative position is not a better answer to the problem of unintended consequences.27 For one, there is no reason to think that the problem of unintended consequences will go away if agents refrain from trying to reform their complex society. Social reform is hardly the only sphere of human activity that generates unintended consequences, as issues like climate change serve to remind us. Nor do we have any reason to expect that reforms will always or even generally lead to worse problems. Such pessimistic expectations are unsupported, as Luban (2020, 78) observes, by “the raw unpredictability implied by the idea of unintended consequences on its own.” Given these facts, the possibility of bad unintended consequences is an acceptable risk for the sake of improving the situation when confronted with real and pressing problems. My point is not that the problem of unintended consequences has no bearing on the pursuit of social reform. Rather, it is that the right response to the problem is not avoiding social reform altogether but managing its risks, for instance, by conducting experiments that limit the number of people potentially affected and that can be halted or reversed (Barrett and Buchanan 2023, 137; Perrow 1999, 304–52; Scott 1998, 345). This may sound like an overly conservative position of its own. But political thinkers of many different stripes have taken the problem of unintended consequences seriously in thinking about how to successfully reform a complex society, even—or especially —when the aim of reform in their view is ultimately to create radically different social arrangements.28 To simply ignore or dismiss the problem would be naïve. Admittedly, these implications of the Complexity View may come across as a disappointment, especially considering the structural injustices of contemporary society. But if the preceding arguments are correct, some

disappointment on this front may be unavoidable if we are to have a compelling explanation of what is distinctive and plausible about the concept of structural injustice. The very issue that distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, namely the complexity of contemporary society and the emergent properties of human actions within it, also sets some important, though surmountable, limits on how agents can remedy it. As is often the case, the definition of the problem delimits the contours of the solution. Filling in these contours, of course, will require further, more fine-grained theoretical and empirical work: investigating specific structural injustices, uncovering their origins in complex webs of human action, and discovering latent possibilities for social reform. Still, by probing the concept of structural injustice itself and asking how it may be defended from recent theoretical challenges, we can come to a clearer view of this prominent concern in contemporary politics.
